questions.q: State the SI unit of electric field and write the formula for the magnitude of electric field due to a point charge \( q \) at distance \( r \).
questions.a: SI unit: N/C (or V/m). Formula: \( E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{|q|}{r^2} \). A wrong answer like "C/N" or missing absolute value on \( q \) reveals confusion between field and force, or ignorance that field magnitude is always positive while direction carries the sign information.

questions.q: A point charge \( +Q \) produces an electric field \( \vec{E} \) at point P. If the charge is replaced by \( -2Q \) at the same location, how does the electric field at P change in magnitude and direction? Explain without calculation.
questions.a: Magnitude doubles (factor of 2) because \( E \propto |q| \). Direction reverses (now radially inward) because the source charge is negative. A student who says "direction stays same" thinks field direction depends only on geometry, not charge sign. A student who says "magnitude halves" confuses the factor of 2 with inverse-square distance dependence.

questions.q: Calculate the electric field at a point 15 cm from a point charge of \( -4.0 \mu C \) in air. Give magnitude and direction. Use \( \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2 \).
questions.a:
Given: \( q = -4.0 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} \), \( r = 0.15 \, \text{m} \), \( k = 9 \times 10^9 \).
Step 1: \( E = k \frac{|q|}{r^2} = (9 \times 10^9) \frac{4.0 \times 10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} \).
Step 2: \( (0.15)^2 = 0.0225 \).
Step 3: \( E = \frac{36 \times 10^3}{0.0225} = 1.6 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).
Direction: radially inward (toward the charge) because \( q \) is negative.
A wrong answer of \( 1.6 \times 10^5 \) N/C indicates a unit conversion error (cm to m). A positive direction indicates sign ignorance.

questions.q: Two point charges \( +3 \mu C \) and \( -3 \mu C \) are placed 20 cm apart on the x-axis at \( x = -10 \) cm and \( x = +10 \) cm. Compare the electric field magnitude at the midpoint (x=0) with that at a point 10 cm to the right of the positive charge (x=20 cm). Which is larger and why?
questions.a:
At midpoint: both fields point toward the negative charge (to the right), so they add. Each has magnitude \( E = k \frac{3\mu C}{(0.1)^2} = 2.7 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \). Total = \( 5.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \).
At x=20 cm: distance to +3 μC is 0.3 m, to -3 μC is 0.1 m. Field from +3 μC points right (away), magnitude \( k \frac{3\mu C}{0.09} = 3 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/C} \). Field from -3 μC points left (toward it), magnitude \( k \frac{3\mu C}{0.01} = 2.7 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \). Net = \( 2.4 \times 10^6 \, \text{N/C} \) left.
Midpoint field is larger. A student choosing x=20 cm likely ignores vector addition or misjudges distances.

questions.q: A student writes: "The electric field due to a point charge is \( \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2} \)." Is this expression correct as a vector equation? If not, correct it and explain the error.
questions.a: The expression is incorrect as a vector equation because the right side lacks a direction vector. The correct vector form is \( \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2} \hat{r} \), where \( \hat{r} \) is the unit vector pointing from the source charge to the field point. The student's version treats \( \vec{E} \) as a scalar. This error leads to sign mistakes when adding fields from multiple charges.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using household items to demonstrate that electric field magnitude decreases with distance from a point-like charged object. Describe the setup, what you would measure, and how you would verify the inverse-square relationship.
questions.a: Rub a plastic ruler with wool to charge it. Suspend a small aluminum foil ball (test charge) on a thread. Bring the ruler near the ball at different measured distances \( r \) and observe the deflection angle \( \theta \). For small angles, \( \tan\theta \approx \theta \propto F \propto E \). Plot \( \theta \) vs \( 1/r^2 \); a straight line through origin confirms inverse-square law. A poor answer would use a large test object (disturbs field) or measure force directly without isolating distance dependence.
